svg.text: The tracheostomy: what changes and what can kill
What the tube bypasses
Air no longer passes the nose and throat, so it
arrives cold, dry and unfiltered. Secretions
thicken and crust, and a crust can block the tube.
Therefore: humidification is treatment, not comfort.
Air also bypasses the vocal cords, so the patient
cannot speak or call out. She cannot summon you
when she is in trouble. Give her a bell and paper.
At the bedside, always, from hour one
A spare tube of the same size
A spare tube one size smaller
Tracheal dilators and a bag-valve mask
Working suction with correct-sized catheters
Humidification, and sterile saline
Checked at every handover and signed for. The
emergency is not the time to find the box is empty.
The patient is distressed and struggling to breathe. Work through it in this order.
1. Is the tube blocked? Pass a suction catheter. If it will not pass, the tube is blocked or displaced.
2. Has it come out? Look and feel at the stoma. A tube that has slipped in front of the trachea moves air
nowhere while looking perfectly in place.
3. Call for help early and give oxygen at the face and at the stoma while you work.
Suction: brief, sterile, and only on the way out
Suction removes oxygen along with secretions. Pre-oxygenate, insert without suction applied, apply suction
only while withdrawing, and keep each pass to a few seconds. Never instil saline routinely to loosen
secretions — it pushes debris downwards and causes desaturation. Humidify instead.
